title: The Midge That Makes the Chocolate

pages.text: On his father’s cocoa farm, Roland loved the pods that hung from the trunks like bright lanterns. “Bees must make all this,” he said, and Marvin, his friend, wrote it down. At school, Mrs Amoo, the agriculture teacher, raised an eyebrow. “Bees?” she said. “Follow me. I will show you who really works for your chocolate.”
sentences: On his father’s cocoa farm, Roland loved the pods that hung from the trunks like bright lanterns.
“Bees must make all this,” he said, and Marvin, his friend, wrote it down.
At school, Mrs Amoo, the agriculture teacher, raised an eyebrow.
“Bees?” she said.
“Follow me.
I will show you who really works for your chocolate.”
pages.alt: A boy and his friend look at a cocoa tree with pods hanging from the trunk.

pages.text: Under a cocoa tree, Mrs Amoo handed Roland a hand lens. “Look at the flower,” she said. Roland saw a tiny five-petalled flower growing straight from the trunk. “It is small,” he said. “And it lasts only a day or two,” said Mrs Amoo. “The flower cannot pollinate itself. It needs an insect small enough to crawl into it. Bees are too big. The workers are biting midges, one to three millimetres long.”

“It is small,” he said.
“And it lasts only a day or two,” said Mrs Amoo.
“The flower cannot pollinate itself.
It needs an insect small enough to crawl into it.
Bees are too big.
The workers are biting midges, one to three millimetres long.”
pages.alt: A boy looks through a hand lens at a tiny cocoa flower on a trunk while a teacher watches.

pages.text: “Midges?” said Marvin, with a face. “Do they bite us?” “Some species do, but the ones that pollinate cocoa are tiny, only a few millimetres long,” said Mrs Amoo. “Cocoa flowers make no nectar, so the midges are not visiting for a meal. They are drawn to the flower and crawl inside, and pollen sticks to them by accident. Scientists are still studying what draws them in. And they are not very efficient. Only about one flower in four hundred to five hundred sets fruit, and only ten to thirty per cent of the pods that start growing reach maturity.” Roland whistled. “So every pod is a small miracle,” he said.

Only about one flower in four hundred to five hundred sets fruit, and only ten to thirty per cent of the pods that start growing reach maturity.” Roland whistled.

pages.alt: A boy and a friend look at a diagram showing tiny midges visiting a cocoa flower.

pages.text: “Now the surprising part,” said Mrs Amoo. She knelt and scooped up a handful of damp, rotting leaves. “The midge’s young, its larvae, live in damp places like this: composting leaf litter and rotting wood on the forest floor. Cocoa grows naturally under taller forest trees. If the shade trees are cut and the leaf litter is swept or burned away, the midges lose their home. Researchers say this may push pollination lower still.”

Cocoa grows naturally under taller forest trees.
If the shade trees are cut and the leaf litter is swept or burned away, the midges lose their home.
Researchers say this may push pollination lower still.”
pages.alt: A teacher holds a handful of damp leaf litter beside a cocoa tree with taller trees above.

pages.text: Roland thought of the day his father cleared some shade trees. “My father wanted more sun for the cocoa,” he said. “Farmers have many reasons,” said Mrs Amoo. “Some want faster growth, others need space or timber. I will not say that all clearing is wrong. But I can say what the midge article says: clearing shade trees harms midge habitat. And reports differ on how much of Ghana’s forest loss is due to cocoa, so we must not blame one cause.”

pages.alt: A boy stands thoughtfully between a cleared area and a shaded part of a cocoa farm.

pages.text: Marvin raised his hand. “So what can farmers do?” Mrs Amoo smiled. “Leave some shade trees, and leave leaf litter on the ground, because that gives the midges a place to breed. These are simple steps that cost little. And ask your extension officer, because they know your soil and your trees.” Roland looked at his notes. “I will tell my father,” he said, “and I will not sweep the litter under the cocoa trees any more.”

pages.text: Marvin printed Roland’s article in the school magazine. “THE TINY WORKERS BEHIND OUR CHOCOLATE. By Roland Bampoe. Many people think bees pollinate cocoa, but the real workers are biting midges only one to three millimetres long. These insects need shade, damp leaf litter and rotting wood in which to breed. Consequently, when farmers clear shade trees and sweep away the litter, they may reduce the number of midges. Farmers can help by keeping some shade trees and leaving the leaf litter. Every pod of cocoa depends on a creature smaller than a grain of rice.”
sentences: Marvin printed Roland’s article in the school magazine.
“THE TINY WORKERS BEHIND OUR CHOCOLATE.
By Roland Bampoe.
Many people think bees pollinate cocoa, but the real workers are biting midges only one to three millimetres long.
These insects need shade, damp leaf litter and rotting wood in which to breed.
Consequently, when farmers clear shade trees and sweep away the litter, they may reduce the number of midges.
Farmers can help by keeping some shade trees and leaving the leaf litter.
Every pod of cocoa depends on a creature smaller than a grain of rice.”
pages.alt: A school magazine page with a headline, byline and a drawing of a tiny midge on a cocoa flower.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: a magazine article has a headline in capitals, a byline with the writer’s name, an opening that catches attention, a body with facts and a clear closing line. It uses formal, clear language with no contractions or slang, and facts that can be checked. Roland’s article uses “consequently” to link cause and effect. Remember to give only facts you are sure of. The end.
